Yes—almost certainly, assuming your eastern horizon is not blocked by buildings, trees, or hills.

At your stated time and location:

- The Moon is about **15° above the eastern horizon** (azimuth ~**87°**, nearly due east).
- It is **98% illuminated**, essentially a full Moon, so it is extremely bright—far brighter than needed for unaided-eye visibility in a clear night sky.
- The Sun is **~31° below the horizon**, well into astronomical night; twilight will not hide it.
- Its separation from the Sun is **~164°**, consistent with a bright waxing-gibbous/near-full Moon visible in the evening.

The only meaningful limitation is its **low altitude**. At 15°, atmospheric extinction, haze, and obstructions near the horizon can reduce contrast, but a nearly full Moon should still be easy to see through ordinary clear air. Look **low in the east, slightly south of due east if necessary**, for a very bright white disk. It may appear somewhat yellow/orange near the horizon.

So: **if you have a reasonably open view toward the east, you should be able to spot it without difficulty.**
